content: Dientamoebiasis is a medical condition caused by an infection with Dientamoeba fragilis, a single-celled parasite that primarily infects the lower gastrointestinal tract in humans. This parasite is recognized as a significant cause of travelers' diarrhea, chronic abdominal pain, persistent fatigue, and growth failure in children. Historically, early microbiologists initially reported that Dientamoeba fragilis was not pathogenic. This conclusion was based on observations from a 1918 study, where six out of seven individuals from whom the organism was isolated were experiencing symptoms of dysentery. However, the researchers determined that the organism was non-pathogenic because it consumed bacteria in culture but did not engulf red blood cells, unlike Entamoeba histolytica, the most well-known pathogenic amoeba at the time. This early report may still influence the hesitancy among physicians to diagnose infections caused by Dientamoeba fragilis. A study conducted in Sydney, Australia, involving 60 individuals with symptomatic Dientamoeba fragilis infections, revealed that all cases were associated with the same genotype of the parasite. Although Dientamoeba fragilis has been described as an infection emerging from obscurity, it has become one of the most prevalent gastrointestinal infections in industrialized countries. This is particularly true among children and young adults. Anyone can become infected with this parasite. However, individuals with weakened immune systems and those living in or traveling to areas with poor sanitation are at a higher risk of infection.
